notes.definition: Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.
explanation: Cells only work properly when the conditions around them are kept within a narrow range. Homeostasis keeps these internal conditions close to their optimum so that enzymes can work at a good rate and all cell functions, such as respiration and protein synthesis, can continue. If conditions drift too far, enzymes may work too slowly or even denature, and cells can be damaged by losing or gaining too much water.

In the human body, homeostasis includes the control of blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels. These conditions are changed all the time by internal changes (for example, respiration releasing energy as heat, or glucose being absorbed after a meal) and by external changes (for example, a cold day or a hot, dry environment). Homeostasis responds to both kinds of change.

Homeostasis is carried out by automatic control systems. You do not have to think about them. These control systems may involve nervous responses, which use electrical impulses carried by neurones, or chemical responses, which use hormones carried in the blood. Some control systems use both.

All control systems include three parts. Receptors are cells that detect stimuli (changes in the environment). Coordination centres, such as the brain, spinal cord and pancreas, receive and process the information from the receptors. Effectors, which are muscles or glands, bring about responses that restore optimum levels.

The information flows in a set order: stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response. Because the response reverses the original change, the condition returns towards its optimum. The receptors keep monitoring, so the level actually fluctuates slightly above and below the optimum rather than staying perfectly constant.
keyFacts: Homeostasis maintains optimum internal conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions.
It responds to both internal and external changes.
In humans it includes control of blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels.
Control systems are automatic and may involve nervous responses or chemical (hormonal) responses.
Receptors are cells that detect stimuli.
Coordination centres (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) receive and process information from receptors.
Effectors are muscles or glands that bring about responses which restore optimum levels.
Order: stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response.
Controlled conditions fluctuate around an optimum within a narrow range.

keyTerms.definition: The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.
A change in the internal or external environment that can be detected by receptors.
A cell (or group of cells) that detects a stimulus.
A structure such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas that receives and processes information from receptors and sends out instructions.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response.
The level of a condition at which cells and enzymes work best.
A system that detects and corrects changes without conscious thought.

workedExamples.title: Identifying the parts of a control system
workedExamples.question: During exercise, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood rises. Cells in the walls of some arteries detect this. Nerve impulses travel to the brain, which sends impulses to the muscles between the ribs and the diaphragm so that breathing gets faster and deeper. Identify the stimulus, receptor, coordination centre, effector and response.
steps: The stimulus is the change being detected: the rise in blood carbon dioxide concentration.
The receptors are the cells in the artery walls that detect the change.
The coordination centre receives and processes the information: the brain.
The effectors carry out the response: the rib (intercostal) muscles and diaphragm, which are muscles.
The response is faster, deeper breathing, which removes more carbon dioxide and returns its concentration towards normal.
workedExamples.answer: Stimulus: rise in carbon dioxide; receptor: cells in artery walls; coordination centre: brain; effectors: rib muscles and diaphragm; response: faster, deeper breathing.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why conditions must be controlled
workedExamples.question: Explain why a large rise in body temperature could stop cells from working properly.
steps: Link the condition to enzymes: reactions in cells are controlled by enzymes.
Enzymes have an optimum temperature (about 37 °C in humans).
Far above the optimum, the shape of the active site changes, so the enzyme is denatured.
The substrate no longer fits, so reactions such as respiration slow down or stop.
workedExamples.answer: Enzymes in cells would denature because their active sites change shape, so the substrate no longer fits and vital reactions such as respiration slow or stop. Homeostasis prevents this by keeping temperature near the optimum.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think homeostasis keeps conditions exactly constant.
misconceptions.right: In fact conditions fluctuate within a narrow range around an optimum, because a change has to happen before it can be detected and corrected.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think receptors are whole organs such as the eye or skin.
misconceptions.right: In fact receptors are cells. The eye and skin are sense organs that contain receptor cells.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse effectors with receptors, saying effectors detect changes.
misconceptions.right: In fact receptors detect stimuli; effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the response.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think homeostasis only responds to the outside environment.
misconceptions.right: In fact it responds to internal changes too, such as heat released by respiration or glucose absorbed after a meal.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all control in the body is done by nerves.
misconceptions.right: In fact control systems may be nervous, chemical (hormones) or a combination of both.

realWorld: Fever: during an infection body temperature can rise several degrees, and doctors monitor it closely because very high temperatures can damage enzymes in the brain.
People with diabetes have a blood glucose control system that does not work properly, so they monitor their blood glucose and use treatments to keep it within a safe range.
Marathon runners in hot weather lose a lot of water in sweat, so their water levels must be restored by drinking to stop cells being damaged by dehydration.
Hospital incubators help premature babies, whose temperature control systems are not fully developed, keep a stable body temperature.
examTips: Learn the exact AQA definition: "the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function in response to internal and external changes".
When asked to identify parts of a control system, remember effectors are always muscles or glands, and receptors are cells that detect stimuli.
Always link homeostasis back to enzymes: say that conditions are kept at the optimum for enzyme action and cell functions.
Write the sequence in the right order: stimulus, receptor, coordination centre, effector, response. Swapping receptor and effector is a common way to lose marks.
In unfamiliar examples, look for the structure that receives information and sends out instructions: that is the coordination centre.
summary: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions at the optimum for enzymes and cell functions.
Humans control blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels.
Control is automatic and may be nervous or chemical.
Receptors detect stimuli; coordination centres (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) process information; effectors (muscles or glands) respond.
Responses restore the optimum, so conditions fluctuate within a narrow range.

flashcards.back: The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.
It keeps optimum conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions.

flashcards.front: Name three conditions controlled by homeostasis in humans.
flashcards.back: Blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels.

flashcards.front: What two types of response can automatic control systems use?

flashcards.back: A cell that detects a stimulus (a change in the environment).

flashcards.front: Give three examples of coordination centres.
flashcards.back: The brain, the spinal cord and the pancreas.

flashcards.front: What does a coordination centre do?
flashcards.back: Receives and processes information from receptors and sends instructions to effectors.
Muscles or glands that bring about responses which restore optimum levels.

flashcards.front: Give the order of a control system.
flashcards.back: Stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response.
A change in the internal or external environment.

flashcards.front: Give an example of an internal change that affects homeostasis.
flashcards.back: Heat released by respiration, or glucose absorbed into the blood after a meal.

flashcards.front: Does homeostasis keep conditions exactly constant?
flashcards.back: No. Conditions fluctuate within a narrow range around the optimum.

questions.question: Which statement best describes homeostasis?
options: The regulation of internal conditions to maintain optimum conditions for function
The response of an organism to changes in its external environment only
The process by which cells divide to replace damaged tissue
The movement of substances from a high to a low concentration
markScheme: 1 mark: regulation of internal conditions to maintain optimum conditions for function
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is about keeping internal conditions at the optimum. It responds to internal and external changes, not just external ones. Cell division and diffusion are different processes.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of an effector?
options: A temperature receptor in the skin
The spinal cord
A muscle
A light-sensitive cell in the eye
markScheme: 1 mark: a muscle
questions.explanation: Effectors are muscles or glands. Receptor cells (in the skin or eye) detect stimuli, and the spinal cord is a coordination centre.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a condition controlled by homeostasis in the human body?
options: Blood glucose concentration
Body temperature
Water levels
Hair colour
markScheme: 1 mark: hair colour
questions.explanation: Blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels are all controlled by homeostasis. Hair colour is an inherited characteristic, not an internal condition that changes and needs regulating.

questions.question: What is the job of a receptor in a control system?
options: To bring about a response
To detect a stimulus
To process information and decide on a response
To carry hormones to target organs
markScheme: 1 mark: to detect a stimulus
questions.explanation: Receptors are cells that detect stimuli. Effectors bring about responses, and coordination centres process information.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the correct order of events in a homeostatic control system?
options: Stimulus → effector → coordination centre → receptor → response
Receptor → stimulus → coordination centre → effector → response
Stimulus → coordination centre → receptor → effector → response
Stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response
markScheme: 1 mark: stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response
questions.explanation: A change (stimulus) must be detected by receptors first. The information goes to the coordination centre, which sends instructions to effectors that produce the response.

questions.question: Which three structures are examples of coordination centres?
options: Brain, spinal cord and pancreas
Brain, muscles and glands
Skin, eye and ear
Liver, muscles and pancreas
markScheme: 1 mark: brain, spinal cord and pancreas
questions.explanation: AQA names the brain, spinal cord and pancreas as coordination centres. Muscles and glands are effectors, and the skin, eye and ear are sense organs containing receptors.

questions.question: Why is it important that human body temperature is kept close to 37 °C?
options: So that the body never loses any energy to the surroundings
Because enzymes in cells work best at around this temperature
So that the blood can carry more oxygen
Because cells stop dividing at any other temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: enzymes work best (optimum) at around this temperature
questions.explanation: Homeostasis keeps optimum conditions for enzyme action. The body always loses some energy to the surroundings, and cell division does not stop at every other temperature.

questions.question: Automatic control systems in the body may involve which two types of response?
options: Voluntary and conscious responses
Nervous responses and chemical responses
Physical responses and genetic responses
Learned responses and reflex responses only
markScheme: 1 mark: nervous and chemical responses
questions.explanation: AQA states that automatic control systems may involve nervous responses or chemical responses (hormones). They are automatic, so they are not conscious.

questions.question: After a meal, cells in the pancreas detect a rise in blood glucose concentration. The pancreas releases insulin, which causes liver cells to take up glucose and store it. In this control system, what acts as the effector?
options: The pancreas, because it releases the insulin
Insulin, because it causes the change
The liver, because it carries out the response
The blood, because it carries glucose
markScheme: 1 mark: the liver
questions.explanation: The effector is the structure that carries out the response that restores the optimum, here the liver taking up and storing glucose. The pancreas is the coordination centre, and insulin is the chemical messenger, not an effector.

questions.question: Which of these is an effector that is a gland?
options: A sweat gland
A receptor cell in the skin
The brain
A nerve cell
markScheme: 1 mark: a sweat gland
questions.explanation: Glands are effectors. Sweat glands produce sweat as a response. Receptor cells detect, the brain coordinates and nerve cells carry impulses.

questions.question: A graph shows that a person's blood glucose concentration rises after a meal and then returns to its original level within two hours. Which is the best explanation?
options: The rise was detected and responses lowered the level back towards the optimum
Glucose was used up by digestion in the stomach
The person's receptors stopped working after the meal
Glucose concentration always stays exactly constant
markScheme: 1 mark: rise detected and response restores optimum
questions.explanation: The rise is a stimulus. It is detected and responses (here hormonal) bring the level back towards the optimum. Glucose is not used by digestion in the stomach, and the graph shows it does change, so it is not exactly constant.

questions.question: Which of these is a cell that acts as a receptor?
options: A muscle cell in the arm
A light-sensitive cell in the retina of the eye
A cell in a sweat gland
A red blood cell
markScheme: 1 mark: light-sensitive cell in the retina
questions.explanation: Receptor cells detect stimuli: light-sensitive cells in the retina detect light. Muscle cells and gland cells are part of effectors. Red blood cells carry oxygen.

questions.question: Which statement about a condition controlled by homeostasis is correct?
options: It stays exactly at the optimum value at all times
It changes randomly with no limits
It fluctuates within a narrow range around the optimum
It only changes when the external environment changes
markScheme: 1 mark: fluctuates within a narrow range around the optimum
questions.explanation: A change must happen before receptors can detect it, so the level rises and falls slightly around the optimum. Internal changes, such as respiration, also affect conditions, not just the external environment.

questions.question: State what is meant by a stimulus.
acceptedAnswers: change in internal or external environment
markScheme: 1 mark: a change in the (internal or external) environment
questions.explanation: A stimulus is any change in the internal or external environment that receptors can detect.

questions.question: Name two conditions in the human body that are controlled by homeostasis.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: blood glucose concentration; body temperature; water levels
questions.explanation: AQA names blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels as conditions controlled in the human body.

questions.question: Name the two types of effector.
markScheme: 1 mark: muscles
1 mark: glands
questions.explanation: Effectors are muscles (which contract) or glands (which secrete substances).

questions.question: Explain why it is important to maintain optimum conditions inside cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: enzymes (work best / are not denatured) at optimum conditions
1 mark: so reactions / cell functions (such as respiration) continue at a suitable rate
questions.explanation: Homeostasis keeps optimum conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions. If conditions change too much, enzymes slow down or denature and cell processes fail.

questions.question: Describe the role of each of the following in a control system: receptors, coordination centres and effectors.
acceptedAnswers: coordination centre receives and processes information
markScheme: 1 mark: receptors (are cells that) detect stimuli / changes
1 mark: coordination centres receive and process information (from receptors)
1 mark: effectors (muscles or glands) bring about responses that restore optimum levels
questions.explanation: Each part has one job: receptors detect, coordination centres process, effectors respond.

questions.question: Give two differences between a nervous response and a chemical response.
markScheme: 1 mark: nervous responses use electrical impulses (in neurones) but chemical responses use hormones (carried in the blood)
1 mark: nervous responses are faster / chemical responses are slower but last longer
questions.explanation: Both are automatic control systems, but nervous responses use electrical impulses along neurones and act quickly for a short time, while chemical responses use hormones in the blood and act more slowly for longer.

questions.question: A person has a fever and their body temperature rises to 41 °C. Suggest and explain why this could be dangerous.
markScheme: 1 mark: temperature is above the optimum for enzymes
1 mark: enzymes denature / active site changes shape
1 mark: substrate no longer fits so reactions (such as respiration) slow or stop / cells cannot function
questions.explanation: At high temperatures the active site of an enzyme changes shape. The substrate no longer fits, so cell reactions slow or stop. This is why homeostasis keeps temperature close to the optimum.

questions.question: On a cold day the external temperature falls by 15 °C, but a healthy person's core body temperature changes by much less than 1 °C. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the change / fall in temperature is detected by receptors
1 mark: coordination centre (brain) causes effectors to respond, which restores the optimum / reverses the change
questions.explanation: Homeostasis responds to external changes. Receptors detect the change and effectors are triggered to reverse it, so core temperature stays within a narrow range.

questions.question: Give one example of an internal change and one example of an external change that could disturb a condition controlled by homeostasis.
markScheme: 1 mark: internal change, for example heat from respiration / glucose absorbed after a meal / exercise
1 mark: external change, for example a hot or cold environment
questions.explanation: Homeostasis responds to both internal changes (inside the body) and external changes (in the surroundings).

questions.question: During exercise, the carbon dioxide concentration in the blood increases. Receptor cells in blood vessels detect this. The brain sends impulses to the breathing muscles, which contract faster. Identify the receptor, the coordination centre and the effector in this example.
markScheme: 1 mark: receptor: cells in the blood vessels
1 mark: coordination centre: the brain
1 mark: effector: the breathing muscles
questions.explanation: Receptors detect the change, the brain processes the information and the muscles (effectors) respond by contracting faster.

questions.question: Explain why receptors in a control system must keep monitoring a condition even after a response has started.
markScheme: 1 mark: so that the coordination centre detects when the level returns to the optimum
1 mark: so the response is reduced / stopped and the level does not go too far the other way
questions.explanation: If monitoring stopped, the effectors could keep responding and push the condition past the optimum in the opposite direction. Continuous monitoring keeps the level within a narrow range.

questions.question: Suggest what would happen to a control system if the receptors were damaged and could not send information to the coordination centre.
markScheme: 1 mark: the change / stimulus would not be detected (so no information reaches the coordination centre)
1 mark: effectors would not respond, so the condition would move away from the optimum / not be restored
questions.explanation: Without information from receptors, the coordination centre cannot trigger a response, so the condition is not corrected.

questions.question: Describe how a control system in the human body responds when a condition moves away from its optimum level. Use an example in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: a change (stimulus) in a condition such as body temperature, blood glucose or water level; receptors (cells) detect the stimulus; information is sent to a coordination centre such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas; the coordination centre processes the information; it sends instructions (by nerves or hormones) to effectors; effectors are muscles or glands; effectors bring about a response that restores the optimum level; example such as rising temperature detected, brain triggers sweat glands.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear sequence from stimulus to response with correct roles for receptor, coordination centre and effector, linked to a relevant example.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct parts of a control system named, but the sequence or roles are unclear, or no example is given.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A good answer follows the information in order and uses an example to show each part: for instance, a rise in blood glucose is detected by the pancreas, which releases insulin, and the liver stores glucose so the level falls.

questions.question: Explain why homeostasis is essential for the survival of cells, and how automatic control systems maintain homeostasis in the human body.
markScheme: Indicative content: cells need optimum conditions for function; enzymes have optimum temperature and pH; too far from optimum, enzymes slow or denature (active site changes shape); cells can be damaged by too much or too little water; body controls blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels; conditions are changed by internal and external changes; control is automatic, by nervous responses (impulses) and/or chemical responses (hormones); receptors detect stimuli; coordination centres (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) receive and process information; effectors (muscles or glands) bring about responses; responses restore optimum; conditions fluctuate within a narrow range.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed explanation linking optimum conditions to enzyme action and cell function, AND a clear, logically ordered description of receptors, coordination centres and effectors, with nervous and chemical responses and at least one example.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some explanation of why conditions matter and a description of most parts of a control system, with some links between them.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example naming a controlled condition or a part of a control system, with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The highest marks go to answers that make two clear links: (1) optimum conditions are needed for enzymes and cell functions, and (2) control systems detect a change and reverse it using receptors, coordination centres and effectors.
